# ꜥnḫ: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **ꜥnḫ** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The First Giving of Life.** In Heliopolitan cosmogony, the creator Atum speaks or sneezes the first gods into being and then gives them life through the ankh.  The sign appears in creation scenes as the instrument by which the sun-god Re enlivens the nostrils of the king and the gods.  It is not a gift from one person to another but the medium of divine animation itself.

**The Breath of the King.** In the daily temple ritual, the cult statue is anointed, dressed, and offered the ankh — life itself — by the officiating priest.  Reliefs at Karnak, Luxor, and Edfu show the king receiving the ankh from Amun, Mut, or Khonsu, a transaction that renews both royal and cosmic vitality.

**The Ankh in the Duat.** The Book of the Dead and the Book of Breathings promise the deceased that they will 'live again' (sꜥnḫ) and breathe by means of the ankh.  Spells equate the amulet with the heart's continued beating and the soul's freedom to move in the afterlife.

## The Name Travels

The ankh outlived pharaonic religion.  Coptic Christians adopted it as the crux ansata, the 'handled cross,' seeing in its loop the triumph of eternal life over death.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **ꜥnḫ** stands at [/ankh/](/ankh/) — [lore](/ankh/lore/), [scholars](/ankh/scholars/), [patterns](/ankh/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can express — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it, mechanically, in Tier-1.
